Decode the Bioreactor

Mechanistic, machine-learning and hybrid models of fed-batch CHO cultures

Author

SDSC STEM4Health hackathon, team 15

Published

November 22, 2026

Summary. Neither a mechanistic model nor a machine-learning model alone predicts the cultures well. The mechanistic ODE gets the shape of a run right but misses batch-to-batch differences (CV MAPE 13.56). Machine learning on its own captures those differences but has no notion of dynamics or mass balance (8.18). Using the ODE as the backbone and learning only its errors combines their strengths (7.98, and down to 7.79 when the two families are averaged). The team’s best model, hybrid v7, scored 6.752 on the leaderboard. The last improvements came from stacking more and more models, and that has real costs in footprint, reproducibility and scientific clarity, which we discuss openly in Section 9.

1 The problem

Each batch is one run of a fed-batch bioreactor: CHO cells grow on a substrate, produce a metabolic byproduct (and later partly consume it), and some of them die. Four feeds are dosed during the run, which raises the volume and dilutes every concentration. For each run we must predict four quantities on each of 13 days:

  • VCD, the viable cell density;
  • TCD, the total cell density (living and dead);
  • substrate concentration;
  • byproduct concentration.

What is given. 61 batches with 14 daily samples each. For 49 batches all measurements are known. For the 12 test batches only the day-0 measurements are given, together with the complete feed schedule and volume log. The task is therefore an initial-value problem with known inputs: from the state at day 0 and the planned feeds, forecast the whole run.

How it is scored. MAPE per variable, averaged over the four. MAPE weights small true values heavily (early cell counts, low byproduct) and punishes over-prediction without bound, so models are best fitted on a log or relative scale.

One subtlety shapes everything that follows. The feeding is adaptive: the main feed (Feed B) tracks the most recent cell count (r = 0.87). Operators dose according to what they measured. The feed log of a test batch therefore partly reveals how well it grew. A data-driven model can exploit this (legitimately: the test feeds are given), but the link runs “more cells → more feed”, not the other way round, so it is not process insight.

2 How we measured progress

All numbers in this report come from one reproducible pipeline (DVC), with every model scored the same way:

Batches Role
39 dev batches 5-fold cross-validation (CV). All model choices are made here.
10 holdout batches One final check per model, never used to choose.
12 test batches Scored by the organisers (leaderboard).

Folds split whole batches, never days of the same batch. A validation batch is predicted exactly like a test batch: from its day-0 values and its feeds only. Anything learned from data (including pooled statistics such as the average feed schedule) is learned inside the training folds. Automated tests check that the holdout never influences fitting.

Decision rule. All models share the same 5 folds, so per-fold differences are far less noisy than the scores themselves. A change was adopted only if it lowered the CV MAPE on average and in at least 4 of the 5 folds. Rejected ideas are logged too (docs/experiments.md).

3 Baselines: how good is “the average run”?

A constant is useless (87.34), but the mean curve per culture day is a strong baseline: 10.61. The runs follow a common recipe, so most of the variance is the shared time course. Every model below has to beat about 10.6.

4 The mechanistic approach

Idea. Write down the biology as ordinary differential equations: Monod-type growth on the substrate, a death rate, substrate uptake, byproduct production and consumption, and the dilution caused by each feed. Fit the kinetic parameters on the training batches, then simulate each new batch forward from its day-0 state and its own feed schedule.

Strengths. The model is physically consistent by construction: concentrations stay positive, feeds enter as mass inputs, dilution is exact, and VCD stays below TCD. Its parameters mean something (a growth rate, a yield), and it can extrapolate to feeding strategies that were never run, which no purely statistical model can claim.

Weaknesses. On its own it is worse than the per-day mean (13.56 vs. 10.61). A handful of shared parameters cannot express how much batches differ from each other, the simplified metabolism misses effects such as the byproduct switch, and errors compound over 13 days of simulation. The figure shows the typical failure: the right shape, at the wrong level.

5 The machine-learning approach

Idea. Treat each sample as a row of features (day, day-0 values, feeds so far, the feed dosed right after the sample) and learn the targets directly, with gradient boosting and ridge regression.

Plain XGBoost barely beats the per-day mean (10.68). Predicting the change relative to day 0 on a log scale helps a little. The real step comes from soft sensors: features computed from each batch’s own logs that act as indirect measurements. Two examples:

  • The unlogged volume. The volume minus the logged feeds, with the sampling losses added back. What remains reflects base addition, and therefore how acidic the culture became (a proxy for byproduct).
  • The substrate bolus. The size of the late substrate top-ups, set by a controller that reacts to the measured substrate. It brackets the substrate level on those days.

With them, ML alone reaches 8.18.

Strengths. Flexible and fast (a fit takes about a second), and it reads batch-level signals from the feed logs, including the operators’ adaptive dosing.

Weaknesses. It knows nothing about dynamics or mass balance. With only 49 labelled batches it cannot learn the physics, so it leans on correlations, some of them reverse-causal (feeding follows growth). It cannot be trusted for a new feeding strategy, and it is weakest exactly where the mechanism is strongest: substrate (9.39 vs. 8.37 for the hybrid below).

6 The hybrid: the ODE as backbone, learning only its errors

Idea. Keep the mechanistic simulation as stage 1: it supplies a physically shaped trajectory for every batch. A stage 2 learns only the correction, the log-ratio between the measurement and the stage-1 prediction, from the soft sensors and the batch’s inputs. Stage 2 blends two branches (a per-day ridge on the sensors and boosted trees) and, for the cell counts, a nearest-neighbour “similar batches” member.

  1. Stage 1: the mechanistic ODE simulates the run from the day-0 state and the feed and volume log.
  2. Soft sensors are computed from the same logs.
  3. Stage 2 learns the correction, log(measured / simulated), from the sensors and the day-0 state.
  4. Forecast = simulation × correction.

Stage 2 is trained on stage-1 predictions for batches stage 1 had not seen (inner folds). The original team code skipped this, which made its CV slightly optimistic. Our version fixes it and learns all pooled statistics inside fit.

Why the combination works. The two families fail in different ways. The ODE’s errors are systematic: a whole batch running high or low, a byproduct switch at the wrong time. These are smooth, low-dimensional, and learnable from a few batch-level signals. Learning the correction is a much easier task than learning the whole trajectory. The data-driven stage never has to discover that cells grow, that feeds dilute, or that substrate is consumed: the ODE provides that for free. It only has to learn how this batch differs. That is why it works with 49 batches.

One finding surprised us. A crude stage 1 (hybrid_lite: a plain ODE without neural nets, fitted in about a minute) is as good as an elaborate one (hybrid_v3: an ODE whose rates are corrected by neural networks, about 15 minutes per fit on 16 cores). Once stage 2 corrects the errors, the details of stage 1 matter little. Its shape matters.

7 Hybrid v7: the team’s best model

Tobias’ hybrid v7 pushes the same idea further: four hybrids with different mechanistic cores, blended per variable and per phase of the run.

  1. A sensor-assimilated Monod core: 400 per-batch parameter draws, weighted by how well each matches the substrate interval implied by the bolus controller and the unlogged volume. The sensors enter the ODE itself rather than only its correction. This was the largest single gain of the whole project.
  2. A functional-PCA trajectory model on the same kind of core.
  3. Hybrid v3.
  4. A two-population core: growing cells switch to a non-growing, byproduct-consuming state.

The weights tell the hybrid story in miniature. Substrate relies on the cores that know the feeding controller. In the growth phase the cell counts and byproduct rely on hybrid v3. Late in the run they shift to the two-population core, which models the transition the other cores miss.

8 Where the remaining error is

Most of the remaining error is a per-batch offset: a whole run is predicted, say, 9% too low on every day. If each batch’s offset were known, the CV MAPE of hybrid_lite would fall from about 8.1 to 6.4. The inputs barely predict these offsets (correlation 0.02 with the feed-B dosing deviation, 0.13 with the day-0 values). Measurement noise puts a floor near 6.2. In other words, the models are now limited by information that is not in the inputs, not by their flexibility. More modelling capacity cannot recover it.

9 The case against stacking more models

The last improvements on the leaderboard came largely from combining models: averaging hybrids, blending four cores with fitted weights, adding finishing models on top. It worked: 7.137 → 6.752 on the leaderboard. But it is worth being honest about what this practice costs.

Footprint. Every layer multiplies the cost of training and serving:

  • An uncached hybrid_v3 fit takes six stage-1 fits of about 15 minutes each on 16 cores (one on all training batches, five inner folds for the stacking). A blend fits all of its members.
  • Hybrid v7 needs four mechanistic cores (one with 400 particles per batch), about 2,000 lines of code in ten scripts, and a chain of cached intermediate files. Rerunning its pinned commit reproduces its CV exactly, but not the submitted file: most predictions agree within 0.2%, one differs by 20%, because an intermediate cache changed between submission and commit. The more layers, the more places for this to happen.
  • For deployment on a controller or a soft-sensor device, a 2 MB ridge + boosting model and a 30 MB, multi-stage, multi-core blend are different engineering propositions.

Diminishing and noisy returns. Averaging hybrid_v3 and hybrid_lite gained 0.05 CV MAPE, because their predictions differ by only 1.4%. Averaging two near-copies adds little. Averaging two genuinely different families (hybrid_blend_ml) gained more (0.16) but improved only 3 of 5 folds, failing our own rule. Tobias’ v6 stack of 17 models scored worse than the 4-model v7. The leaderboard has only 12 batches. When two candidates differ by 1-2% per prediction, a ±0.3 change in score is noise, and we saw both directions.

It is unprincipled. Each extra layer is chosen because it lowered a score, on the same folds that report the score. Blend weights per variable and per phase, the choice among candidate sets, the finishing steps: every choice spends a little of the validation set’s honesty. Tobias estimates about 0.03 MAPE of optimism from choosing among six 4-model sets alone. More importantly, a stack does not explain anything. We cannot read a growth rate or a yield from a geometric blend of four corrected simulators. Without the forecast accuracy, the model gives no answer to why a batch behaves as it does, and that was half of the challenge’s brief.

What we would keep. The gains that came from ideas rather than layers are the ones that generalise: soft sensors that turn the feed and volume logs into indirect measurements, assimilating them into the ODE, and the hybrid structure itself. A defensible final model is one mechanistic core with sensor assimilation plus one learned correction. It is small enough to audit, fit and deploy, and within a few tenths of the best stack.

10 Reproducibility

  • One pipeline. dvc repro rebuilds every number and figure in this report from the raw data, the frozen split, the code and params.yaml. DVC reruns only what changed.
  • Versioned models. Model versions are git tags in a registry (GTO), not “_v2” file names. Each tag points at the commit whose code, parameters and lock file produced it. Hybrid v7 runs from a pinned commit of its own branch.
  • Logged decisions. Every experiment, including the rejected ones, is recorded with its per-fold result in docs/experiments.md.
  • No data in git. Only hashes of the challenge data, and no file in reports/ contains measured values.

11 Limitations and next steps

  • Our CV (5 folds, 39 batches) and Tobias’ (7 folds, 49 batches) are different protocols. Hybrid v7 has no predictions for our holdout batches, so it is compared on the leaderboard only.
  • Data-driven parts exploit the adaptive feeding, which helps the forecast but would break under a new feeding strategy. A deployment for process design should restrict stage 2 to causal inputs, or at least test it on feeding schedules outside the historical range.
  • Next steps, in order of expected value: a single sensor-assimilated core with a learned correction as the reference model; interpretable reporting of the fitted kinetic parameters per batch; and asking for online sensor data (pH, dissolved oxygen, base addition), which would attack the per-batch offsets directly.
